metric.why: Annual matching and hourly matching are very different claims; hourly carbon-free matching is the harder standard the largest operators now report progress against. Reading which claim is being made matters more than the percentage.
metric.definition: The share of facility consumption matched by renewable generation, reported either as annual matching through purchased certificates or as around-the-clock hourly matching.

reading.body:
Annual and hourly renewable matching are fundamentally different claims, and which one a data center reports shapes what its renewable energy figure actually means.

Annual matching allows a facility to consume fossil power during peak hours and offset it by purchasing certificates for renewable generation elsewhere in the year. Hourly matching requires the facility to source renewable power continuously, aligned with consumption in real time. The harder standard reveals whether a data center can actually run on renewables when demand peaks, rather than whether it balances the books on an annual ledger. Operators reporting hourly progress are making a stronger claim about their infrastructure.

This distinction matters because data centers now consume power at scales that stress regional grids. A facility claiming 100 percent annual renewable matching may still draw from coal plants during hours when solar does not generate. An hourly matcher must either have on-site generation, nearby renewable sources available on demand, or storage capacity. For AI workloads that run compute continuously, hourly matching is the metric that tests whether the underlying power infrastructure can sustain growth without building new fossil capacity.

The metric does not reveal how much total power a data center consumes, whether it has actually built new renewable capacity or only purchased rights to existing generation, or whether hourly matching is achieved through storage, proximity to renewables, or load shifting. It measures how consumption is reported, not the physical grid constraints that will determine whether regions can support the next wave of AI infrastructure expansion.
